Science.title: Close-up images show defects locking electrons into stable Wigner solids

The team's methodology included an innovative simulation tool that enabled accurate theoretical interpretations of its experimental observations.

Science.title: NASA’s New Horizons spots signs of liquid nitrogen flowing on Pluto
Science.summary: Scientists have found the first evidence that liquid may have flowed across Pluto’s surface in the recent past. Dark features on the enormous Sputnik Planitia glacier appear consistent with liquid nitrogen rising through cracks from deep beneath the ice. Computer models show that nitrogen could melt at the glacier’s base and travel upward like fluid through small conduits. The finding reveals that Pluto may be much more geologically active than its frozen appearance suggests.

Science.title: Why global wind energy may stay steady even as storm tracks shift poleward
Science.summary: Understanding how wind changes in response to global warming is necessary for accurately modeling climate and weather, identifying risks to infrastructure, and assessing global wind power capacity.

Science.title: How fast are you ageing? Ask AI
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02913-7 A new system will help scientists to refine large language models for longevity research and clarify ‘biological’ age.

Science.title: 1,000-year-old 'snake amulet' featuring a Christian saint and 'Medusa' discovered in Russia
Science.summary: Archaeologists discovered the two-sided pendant, which features a snake-slaying saint and a snake-haired woman, during an excavation in northwestern Russia.

Science.title: Electron and photon beams drive same gold-forming reaction toward different nanoscale structures
Science.summary: Beauty and mystery—it is hard to imagine a more alluring combination, and this is precisely what we encounter when we observe phenomena in the nanoworld. But are we really sure that observations made using modern microscopic techniques do not influence what is happening there? A comparison of images of copper oxide nanoparticles reacting with chloroauric acid, obtained using electron and photon beams, has yielded unexpected results.

Science.title: 'At some point we're going to have to react': How El Niño, climate change, and crime are pushing the Amazon rainforest over the brink
Science.summary: Live Science spoke with Amazon researcher Bernardo Flores about how El Niño could help drive Earth's largest tropical rainforest past a globe-altering tipping point.

Science.title: Laser shocks turn plastic into ultra-small, high-purity nanodiamonds
Science.summary: Nanodiamonds are tiny diamond particles that usually measure mere millionths of a millimeter. They are extremely hard, stable and heat-resistant and highly adaptable for various purposes in medicine, new materials, catalysis and energy technology. By compressing plastic with lasers, researchers at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) and the University of Rostock are now able to systematically produce high-purity, ultra-small diamonds with a narrow size distribution. Science.title: Chemists overturn 40-year assumption about a key class of superconductors
Science.summary: Scientists at Warwick have shown that a material treated for 40 years as a uniform, textbook superconductor is in fact a patchwork of different crystal structures throughout its bulk, using an advanced 3D imaging technique to see deep inside the crystal for the first time.

Science.title: Disorder is key to tuning a high-temperature superconductor
Science.summary: Cornell physicists have discovered that minimizing disorder, not varying electron count, is the key factor for controlling superconductivity in the unique material iron selenide (FeSe), a new insight for understanding high-temperature superconductors.

Science.title: 1,700-year-old fragment of the 'Odyssey' discovered in Dutch library
Science.summary: An expert in ancient Greek literature identified a fragment of the "Odyssey" among a collection of manuscripts in a Dutch university library.

Science.title: Take a risk or play it safe? Neuronal tug-of-war helps the brain decide
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02911-9 Using a video game involving bombs and treasure chests, researchers show how neural activity flickers between two regions of the frontal cortex when the brain weighs up a tricky decision.

Science.title: A space shark, 'royal' auroras and a 'Venusian pearl': See the winners of the 2026 ZWO Astronomy Photographer of the Year contest
Science.summary: A Royal Observatory Greenwich contest showcased work from around the night sky and the solar system, with prize-winning photos spanning topics ranging from auroras to planets.

Science.title: Europe's earliest glacier loss day in years signals a reckoning for the Alps
Science.summary: On June 29, 2026, the snow accumulated by Switzerland's glaciers over the course of the previous winter had melted. Known as Glacier Loss Day, this date marks the point at which further melting begins to erode the glaciers' mass until snow accumulation resumes in the fall. Matthias Huss, the network head of Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS), told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that this year's Glacier Loss Day was "three months too early, compared to a healthy state."

Science.title: Scaling up the detection of genome-edited rice lines
Science.summary: A new open-access study introduces RiSpy, a data-driven fingerprinting framework that makes the identification of genome-edited (GE) rice lines more robust, scalable and broadly applicable. Researchers from Sciensano, together with CIRAD and DARWIN project partners, in collaboration with colleagues from Ghent University, have presented the new methodological framework for the reliable identification of genome-edited (GE) rice lines in the journal Briefings in Bioinformatics.

Science.title: A finely tuned mess—how disorder can make networks more stable
Science.summary: Perfection is overrated—at least when it comes to complex systems like the power grid, food webs and advanced materials. For decades, scientists generally assumed that networks function most reliably when their individual components are as similar as possible. But real-world networks are rarely uniform.

Science.title: Report on global water resources: Worldwide continents are drying up
Science.summary: The global water cycle is becoming increasingly unbalanced. Extreme droughts and floods are the result. This is shown in this year's report by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on the state of global water resources, "State of Global Water Resources 2025," which was published today.

Science.title: Climate change contributing to permafrost thawing and glacial thinning
Science.summary: An international team of glaciologists and climate scientists, including professor Bethan Davies from Newcastle University, carried out a rapid scientific analysis and identified the role of climate change and its impacts on the high-altitude landscape.

Science.title: New bioinformatics tools help identify pathogenic variants in the genome
Science.summary: Structural variants and so-called tandem repeats are individual differences in the human genome. They are increasingly linked to diseases, but analyzing and interpreting them poses challenges for researchers.

Science.title: Moles' wide-armed posture reshapes how their shoulder bones carry loads
Science.summary: While the scapula is the primary bone supporting the body in terrestrial quadrupedal mammals, an analysis of internal bone structure in underground moles (family Talpidae) showed a more important role for the clavicle.

Science.title: New mesothelioma drug turns cancer’s own defenses against it
Science.summary: Scientists are testing a counterintuitive way to fight mesothelioma, an aggressive asbestos-linked cancer with few effective treatments. A new experimental mesothelioma drug kills cancer cells by disabling PRX3, an antioxidant defense that tumors use to survive intense oxidative stress. In an early clinical trial, it controlled disease progression in 67% of patients and produced encouraging survival results, raising hopes that the strategy could eventually be used against other cancers.

Science.title: 'Predatory behavior': Elite mathematicians clash over OpenAI's 'solution' to million-dollar math problem
Science.summary: OpenAI's controversial claim to have cracked the Navier-Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem has sent shock waves through the mathematics community.

Science.title: Scientists name a new cat species for the first time in over a century
Science.summary: The South American tiger cat is not one species but five distinct species, a new study finds.

Science.title: Scientists identify rare genetic mutation that dramatically raises risk of lung cancer in nonsmokers
Science.summary: A genetic mutation that raises lung cancer risk was much more common among those born in Southeastern states than elsewhere in the U.S.

Science.title: Identifying old-growth forests in Northern Europe requires common scientific criteria
Science.summary: Old-growth forests are some of Europe's most valuable natural ecosystems, but they are also among the most threatened. Their role in conserving biodiversity, regulating the climate, preserving cultural heritage and supporting people's well-being is invaluable. According to a rough estimate, only around 3% of Europe's forests meet the criteria for primary or old-growth forests, and their extent continues to decline rapidly in Northern Europe.

Science.title: Who gets credit in the AI era? OpenAI maths bombshell sparks debate
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02910-w Controversy around OpenAI’s claim to have solved the Navier–Stokes problem highlights how researchers could be inadvertently sharing — and absorbing— ideas through chatbots.

Science.title: Passion Meets Precision at NASA’s Flight Research Lab
Science.summary: Long before they helped shape NASA’s future aerospace breakthroughs, Derek Abramson, Justin Hall, and Justin Link were in their garages and homes building radio‑controlled aircraft, testing new ideas, and flying their creations at hobby events. That early passion now fuels the work of NASA’s Dale Reed Subscale Flight Research Laboratory at the agency’s Armstrong Flight […]

Science.title: Circular economy pilot projects show hotels can reduce waste and costs
Science.summary: The new EU Packaging Regulation (PPWR) has been in effect since Aug. 12, 2026. Under this regulation, beginning in January 2030, the food service industry may no longer buy food or toiletries packaged in single-use plastic—for example, ketchup packets or individually wrapped bars of soap. This is increasing pressure on hotels, restaurants and catering businesses to act.

Science.title: Developing new asymmetric catalytic reactions for the synthesis of complex molecules
Science.summary: Do Hyun Ryu's research team in the Department of Chemistry at Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) has developed two new asymmetric catalytic methods for the precise synthesis of complex molecules using chiral organic catalysts.

Science.title: Motivational traits may help explain why some people report greater well-being
Science.summary: "People who are determined, passionate and believe in their ability to improve appear more likely to flourish and experience meaningful, engaging lives," says Professor Hermundur Sigmundsson at NTNU's Department of Psychology.

Science.title: Transfer learning corrects alloy calculations to predict unexplored materials
Science.summary: Metals can be transformed into alloys by adding different elements, allowing their strength, stability and other properties to be tailored. A key parameter for understanding these properties is the volume size factor (VSF), which quantifies lattice distortion caused by differences in atomic size.

Science.title: This sponge has holes. Some find that truly disgusting
Science.summary: Imagine you're scrolling through TikTok and come across an image of a lotus seed pod or sponge.

Science.title: Summer Goes Out With a Heat Dome
Science.summary: Temperature records toppled across the central and southern U.S. as the autumnal equinox approached.

Science.title: Schoolhouse meals serve up an income bump
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02896-5 Modelling shows a link between feeding programmes and higher potential earning in five African nations.

Science.title: JWST’s mysterious little red dots may be black holes growing at incredible speeds
Science.summary: New supercomputer simulations suggest JWST’s puzzling Little Red Dots are rapidly growing black holes from the early Universe. Extreme radiation may have helped create unusually massive black hole seeds, while dense surrounding gas allowed them to grow dozens of times faster than black holes can today. The simulated objects closely resemble the Little Red Dots seen by Webb. If correct, they could solve the mystery of how enormous black holes formed so soon after the Big Bang.

Science.title: Newfound fungal nutrient-sensing mechanism could advance biofuels and disease control
Science.summary: Scientists have taken a step toward a better understanding of how fungi sense and respond to nutrients in the environment, which is critical for engineering fungi for green technologies and combating fungal pathogens and their resistance to treatments.

Science.title: Exclusive: New evidence for hidden chambers beyond Tutankhamun’s tomb
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02621-2 Geophysical survey yields ‘tantalizing’ data that could point to Nefertiti’s burial place – but it’s too early to draw definitive conclusions.

Science.title: A new rulebook for designing stable dilute alloy catalysts
Science.summary: Dilute alloy catalysts could improve fuel, plastic and pharmaceutical production, but their instability under heat holds back widespread use. Researchers at University of Michigan Engineering built a stability rulebook for this class of materials, which are made of a tiny amount of an active dopant metal dispersed in an inert host metal. A study outlining the rulebook was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.
